findings.title: Pre-existing local recovery-codes credential is left in place (and still valid) when the user storage accepts the new codes
findings.body: `createRecoveryCodesCredential` calls `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)` and, if the user storage accepts it, never touches the local store. Recovery codes are a single-credential type: the local `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.createCredential` path replaces whatever credential of that type exists. With this helper, a federated user who already has a recovery-codes credential in the Keycloak DB (e.g. created before the storage started supporting this type, or after a storage upgrade) will keep it when regenerating codes. Because `UserCredentialManager.isValid` falls through to the local credential providers whenever the user storage's `isValid` returns false, the old locally stored codes remain usable for login indefinitely, and the admin/account UIs will show two recovery-code credentials. The helper should remove any existing local `recovery-authn-codes` credential when the storage path succeeds (or at least document that storages must handle this).

findings.title: Local-store removal is applied to a credential that may come from the user storage
findings.body: `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential` now returns the federated credential (from `getFederatedCredentialsStream()`) in preference to the local one, but the follow-up logic is unchanged: when `allCodesUsed()` is true it calls `authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId())`. For a credential that lives in the external user storage this does not remove anything there (it targets the Keycloak-managed credential table), so the exhausted credential stays and `isConfiguredFor` keeps returning true. Worse, credential models produced by storages typically have no id (the test provider builds them via `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues`, which leaves `id` null), so `removeStoredCredentialById(null)` reaches `em.find(..., null)` and throws `IllegalArgumentException`, failing the login after the code was already validated. The federated case should call `disableCredentialType(...)` on the storage (or skip the removal) instead.

findings.title: Login form hard-depends on storages returning recovery credentials in Keycloak's internal JSON format (or at all)
findings.body: The bean (and `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator` line 83) feeds whatever `getFederatedCredentialsStream()` returns straight into `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel`, which deserializes `credentialData`/`secretData` as `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialData`/`RecoveryAuthnCodesSecretData` and wraps any `IOException` in a `RuntimeException`. A user storage that accepted the codes via `updateCredential` (it receives them as a plain JSON array in `challengeResponse`) and exposes them in its own format, or that validates via `isValid`/`isConfiguredFor` but does not override `getCredentials`, will cause either a 500 while rendering the recovery-code login page or a `NoSuchElementException` from the unguarded `credentialModelOpt.get()`. This undocumented contract is only satisfied by the test provider because it re-hashes the raw codes with `createFromValues` in `getCredentials`. The code should handle an empty Optional/unparseable model gracefully (e.g. fall back to code number 0 or an error message) and the required storage contract should be documented.

findings.title: User label and generation timestamp are dropped when the credential goes to the user storage
findings.body: The `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` built in `RecoveryAuthnCodesAction` carries the user-supplied label and the `generatedAt` timestamp, but the `UserCredentialModel("", type, recoveryCodesJson)` handed to `updateCredential` only carries the raw codes. A storage therefore cannot preserve the label/creation time the user chose (the test provider ends up with `userLabel == null` and a storage-side timestamp), so the credential shown in the admin/account consoles for federated users differs from what the user entered.

findings.title: Backwards-compatibility provider is extended with new-API code, defeating its purpose
findings.body: The class Javadoc states this provider is a frozen Keycloak 4.8.3 implementation that must keep working without code changes, which is what `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorageTest` is meant to prove. This PR adds an override of `CredentialInputUpdater.getCredentials` (an API that did not exist in 4.8.3), uses `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel`/`KeycloakModelUtils.generateId()`, and changes the OTP path to assign an id. After this change the test no longer demonstrates that an unmodified legacy provider still works; it only demonstrates that a provider written against the current API works. The recovery-code support should live in a separate test provider (or the Javadoc/intent of this class must be revised).

findings.title: Test storage accepts any stored code, never consumes codes, and keeps them in plaintext
findings.body: `isValid` for `recovery-authn-codes` returns true if the input matches *any* of the stored codes and never removes the used one; `getCredentials` rebuilds the model from the full list each time, so `getNextRecoveryAuthnCode()` always yields code 0. Consequently `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` can only ever assert `expectedCode == 0` and does not exercise code consumption, the `allCodesUsed()` branch, or the required-action re-trigger for a federated credential, which are exactly the paths the production changes touched. Also, `getCredentials` dereferences `getMyUser(user)` without the null check used elsewhere in this class, so an unknown user yields an NPE instead of an empty stream.

findings.title: Recovery-code login is never completed, so the final logout is a no-op
findings.body: Unlike the OTP tests in this class, `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` calls `enterRecoveryAuthnCodePage.clickSignInButton()` and then `testAppHelper.logout()` without first calling `testAppHelper.completeLogin()`. `TestAppHelper.logout()` logs out using the refresh token obtained in `completeLogin()`; without it the logout request is sent without a token, fails, and the result is not asserted. The authorization code is never exchanged either, so the test does not verify the login actually yields tokens, and the browser SSO session for `otp1` is left behind for subsequent tests in the class.
